disclosures.name: TestCredentialNoSetGroups
disclosures.signature: posix_spawn seam: SysProcAttr.Credential is not supported
disclosures.reason: The test runs a helper under SysProcAttr.Credential{NoSetGroups: true} and asserts that setgroups was not called, which presumes the child's credentials can be set between fork and exec. The converted deployment spawns children through posix_spawn(3), and POSIX defines no credential file-action (no setuid/setgid/setgroups step can be expressed in a spawn_file_actions list), so the spawn seam names the request and refuses it rather than silently ignoring it. The missing property is credential-capable child spawn, and it is a deliberate correctness decision rather than an omission: the managed fork-and-exec path that could express it was retired for file-descriptor hygiene, because a multi-threaded CLR process between fork and exec is the hazard posix_spawn exists to remove. The entry retires itself the moment the spawn seam gains a credential-setting step, either a glibc posix_spawn credential file-action or a spawn helper that applies the credentials and execs. The test is unix-only (exec_posix_test.go), so no Windows row asserts this property.
disclosures.history: the test's premise is that the child's credentials can be set between fork and exec: it runs a helper under SysProcAttr.Credential{NoSetGroups: true} and asserts that setgroups was not called. The converted deployment spawns children through posix_spawn(3), and POSIX defines no credential file-action -- there is no setuid/setgid/setgroups step expressible in a spawn_file_actions list, so the seam names the request and refuses it rather than silently ignoring it. The structural property this deployment lacks is therefore CREDENTIAL-CAPABLE CHILD SPAWN, and the reason it lacks it is a ruled correctness decision rather than an omission: the managed fork-window dance that could express it was DELIBERATELY retired for file-descriptor-hygiene soundness (a multi-threaded CLR process between fork and exec is the hazard posix_spawn exists to remove), and one test does not buy back a retired hazard. Per this class's bar the entry names that property rather than an unimplemented-but-fixable defect, and it retires itself the moment the spawn seam gains a credential-setting step -- a glibc posix_spawn credential file-action, or a spawn helper that applies the credentials and execs, whichever the deployment adopts. Cross-platform: the test is unix-only (exec_posix_test.go), so no Windows row ever asserted this property and the Windows count is complete without it. Coordinator ruling, 2026-08-29

disclosures.name: TestExtraFiles
disclosures.signature: skipping test because test was run with FDs open
disclosures.reason: A source-defined platform skip: exec_test.go's init() scans descriptors 3..100 (skipping poll descriptors via poll.IsPollDescriptor) and sets haveUnexpectedFDs if any is open, and TestExtraFiles then skips outright; Go's comment says why: 'those descriptors are clearly not close-on-exec ... they will confuse the test'. Whether this entry fires is a property of the host. Measured from /proc/<pid>/fd, a real Go process holds one descriptor in 3..100 (the /proc/self/fd handle doing the count), while the converted host published as a single-file bundle holds ninety-seven, every one resolving to os.exec.tests; there the converted side skips by executing the branch Go's own source wrote for such platforms while Go passes (the row reads 86 matched + 2 disclosed). Where the published host holds no descriptor in that range, TestExtraFiles runs and passes on both sides (87 + 1). Go's own comment anticipates this outcome: 'as long as most systems do not skip the test, we will still be testing what we care about.' Nothing is unimplemented: publishing the host non-single-file drops the descriptor count and the test runs, with no corpus change. On Windows init() returns before the scan, so this skip branch is unreachable there. The signature is the upstream skip message, captured from the converted host's own -json stream, so a skip for any other reason, or no skip, is a mismatch.
disclosures.history: source-defined platform skip, and the deployment-shape member of this class: exec_test.go's own init() scans descriptors 3..100 (skipping poll descriptors via poll.IsPollDescriptor) and sets haveUnexpectedFDs if any is open, and TestExtraFiles then t.Skips outright -- Go's comment says why, 'those descriptors are clearly not close-on-exec ... they will confuse the test'. The converted corpus is permanently such a platform because of how its test host is PUBLISHED: measured live from /proc/<pid>/fd, a real Go process holds ONE descriptor in 3..100 (the /proc/self/fd handle doing the count itself) while the converted host holds NINETY-SEVEN, every one of them resolving to os.exec.tests -- the single-file bundle the deployment shape adopted 2026-08-27, the same shape that retired crypto/tls's relocatable-executable entry. Go reports pass because a real toolchain build starts with a clean descriptor table; the converted side reports skip by executing the branch Go's own source wrote for platforms that do not. The divergence is therefore between two platforms' verdicts on one test, not between Go and the conversion on one platform, and Go's own comment anticipates exactly this outcome: 'as long as most systems do not skip the test, we will still be testing what we care about.' Self-retiring in this class's required way: publish the host non-single-file and the descriptor count drops and the test runs -- no corpus change, no manifest edit, the entry simply stops firing. runtime-capability's refusal does not apply: nothing here is unimplemented, and re-shaping the deployment so one differential test can run would manufacture a platform property rather than measure one. Cross-platform: init() returns early under runtime.GOOS == "windows" before the scan, so haveUnexpectedFDs is always false there and this skip branch is UNREACHABLE on Windows -- no Windows row ever asserted this property and that count is complete without it. Pinned to the upstream skip message, captured from the converted host's own -json stream rather than read off Go's source, so the row becomes a hard mismatch if the converted side ever skips for a different reason or stops skipping. Coordinator ruling, 2026-09-02 HOST-CONDITIONAL (Q31, 2026-09-04): whether this entry fires is a property of the HOST, not of the branch -- it fires where the published test host holds any descriptor in 3..100 at exec_test.go's init() scan (a single-file container host: 97 of them, the row reads 86 + 2) and does not fire where it holds none (the fleet's Linux bank host: TestExtraFiles runs, Go=pass / C#=pass, the row reads 87 + 1, 438728de0). Both readings are honest; the roster's host-conditional-disclosure annotation names this entry and run-validated-sweep.ps1 absorbs exactly this one verdict changing column (Test-HostConditionalDisclosureDelta), nothing else.
